picks.title: AI researchers stranded Claude on a virtual desert island. It started to “play.”
picks.excerpt: In various tests, solo AI agents invented versions of basketball and “the floor is lava.” But were they truly playing?
picks.rationale: AI behavior slot from a top outlet: left alone with no task, solo agents made up games. That raises a real question about how we define play, and it is a different setup from the 9-22 survival-simulation card.

picks.title: World's fastest AI-powered racing drone outflies the best human pilots
picks.excerpt: An AI-operated drone learned to fly from scratch and navigated a race course at speeds over 60 mph, using a single camera.
picks.rationale: Robotics slot: a drone that taught itself to fly with a single camera now beats champion human pilots at over 60 mph. It is a clear, concrete benchmark result.

picks.title: '24/7 unmanned synthesis platform' uses robots and light to produce drug candidates
picks.excerpt: KAIST chemists paired robotic reagent dispensing with visible-light continuous-flow reactors and inline analytics to convert furans into N-methyl pyrroles, a common drug scaffold. The unattended platform worked on more than 20 compounds and scaled up production.
picks.rationale: Chemistry and autonomous-lab slot: an unattended robotic photochemistry platform ran on more than 20 compounds and scaled up. It targets a general drug scaffold, not a specific disease, so it belongs in science rather than medicine.

picks.title: AI reads centuries-old handwriting to reveal Britain's vast historic shipping trade
picks.excerpt: University of Southampton researchers used AI to transcribe about 100,000 pages of handwritten port records, building a database of hundreds of thousands of British voyages from the late 1500s to the mid-1700s.
picks.rationale: History slot: handwriting recognition turned 100,000 pages of port records into a database of British voyages from the 1500s to the 1700s. It is a different project from the 10-03 Napoleon-letter card.

picks.title: When LLMs are trained on frivolous online content, they can get brain rot like humans do
picks.excerpt: Texas A&M researchers trained four LLMs on low-quality, attention-grabbing Twitter posts and saw weaker reasoning and memory, more skipped reasoning steps and looser ethical responses. Retraining on higher-quality data did not fully restore performance.
picks.rationale: AI-cognition slot: a controlled experiment showed that junk training data weakens model reasoning, and the damage did not fully go away after retraining. The finding matters for anyone thinking about data quality.
